claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Freed et al., 2015, Maruyama, 2015, and Moriki et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Ligand-induced conformational changes transform pre-formed receptor tyrosine kinase dimers into a state competent for autophosphorylation.
claims.source: Many receptor tyrosine kinases, for example, have been observed as pre-formed, inactive dimers. Ligand-induced conformational changes transform these receptors into a state in which they are competent of autophosphorylation (Freed et al., 2015; Maruyama, 2015; Moriki et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Freed et al., 2015, Maruyama, 2015, and Moriki et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Other kinases can be locally concentrated on a membrane by their specific binding to a lipid second messenger, thereby facilitating autophosphorylation.
claims.source: Other kinases can be locally concentrated on a membrane by their specific binding to a lipid second messenger, thereby facilitating autophosphorylation (Chung et al., 2019; Levina et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2019, Levina et al., 2022, and Wang et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Early kinetic data indicated that autophosphorylation of IRK could occur in both cis and trans.
claims.source: Early kinetic data indicated that autophosphorylation of IRK could occur in both cis (Shoelson et al., 1991; Yamada et al., 1992) and trans (Cobbs et al., 1989; Frattali et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Shoelson et al., 1991, Yamada et al., 1992, Cobbs et al., 1989, and Frattali et al., 1992.

claims.claim: Structural and biochemical studies of IGFR1 and FGFR3 have concluded that the autophosphorylation reaction occurs in trans.
claims.source: However, structural and biochemical studies of related kinases, including insulin-like growth factor receptor 1 (IGFR1) and fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), have since concluded that the reaction occurs in trans (Chen et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2020 and Wu et al., 2008.

claims.claim: IGFR1 has been trapped in a symmetric dimer in which the activation loop of both protomers is in the active site of the opposing protomer.
claims.source: Indeed, evidence that this reaction can be performed in trans has been obtained from a number of crystal structures in which the activation loop of both protomers (Wu et al., 2008) (symmetric, Figure 8D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2008 and shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: FGFR3 has been trapped in an asymmetric dimer in which the activation loop of just one protomer is in the active site of the opposing protomer.
claims.source: Indeed, evidence that this reaction can be performed in trans has been obtained from a number of crystal structures in which the activation loop of both protomers (Wu et al., 2008) (symmetric, Figure 8D) or just one (Chen et al., 2020) (asymmetric, Figure 8E) is trapped in the active site of the opposing protomer.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: IGFR1 has also been trapped in an asymmetric dimer that is different from the FGFR1 asymmetric dimer, yet still positions the activation loop tyrosine for phosphoryl transfer.
claims.source: The promiscuity of lattice contacts is further evidenced by the trapping of IGFR1 in an asymmetric dimer that is again different from the FGFR1 asymmetric dimer, yet still positions the activation loop tyrosine for phosphoryl transfer (Nemecek et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Nemecek et al., 2010 and Xu et al., 2015.

claims.claim: A two-step trans-autophosphorylation mechanism has been proposed for PAK and IRAK4 based on their crystal structures.
claims.source: While IGFR1 might accomplish trans-autophosphorylation of each protomer simultaneously, FGFR3 would presumably need to go through a two-step reaction mechanism. Such a mechanism has also been proposed for other kinases, including p21-activated kinase (PAK) and Interleukin 1 (IL-1) receptor-associated kinase 4 (IRAK4), based on their crystal structures (Ferrao et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferrao et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The kinase domain of IRAK1 has been proposed to form heterodimers with phosphorylated, but not unphosphorylated, IRAK4, leading to a model in which IRAK4 phosphorylates IRAK1.
claims.source: Interestingly, the kinase domain of IRAK1, which apparently does not homodimerize, has been proposed to form heterodimers with phosphorylated, but not unphosphorylated, IRAK4, leading to a model in which IRAK4 phosphorylates IRAK1 (Wang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The activation loop adopts the same conformation in cis, trans symmetric, trans asymmetric, and trans substrate structures, with the tyrosine poised for phosphate transfer from ATP.
claims.source: Zooming in on the conformation of the activation loop surrounding the phosphorylated tyrosine in the cis, trans symmetric, trans asymmetric, and trans substrate structures reveals that the activation loop adopts the same conformation in each case, with the tyrosine poised for transfer of phosphate from ATP to its hydroxyl group (Figure 8H).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8H and describes structural observations.

claims.claim: Cis, trans symmetric, trans asymmetric, and trans substrate reactions are all stereochemically possible based on crystal structures.
claims.source: We can, therefore, conclude from these structures that cis, trans symmetric, trans asymmetric, and trans substrate reactions are all stereochemically possible.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claims.claim: What we see in a crystal lattice and what we can observe in a test tube do not necessarily reflect reality in the cell.
claims.source: Does that mean that they can all happen in the cell? The answer to this question is more complicated and depends on the factors that limit each of these reactions, including local concentration and the available conformational space that can be sampled. Many of these mechanisms are surely rooted in strong biochemical evidence, but, once again, we should be careful not to let our eyes deceive us: what we see in a crystal lattice and what we can observe in a test tube do not necessarily reflect reality in the cell.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of in vitro data.

results.result: Protein kinases are ubiquitous signal transducers in eukaryotic cells that use ATP to phosphorylate substrates. The phosphoryl-transfer mechanism is universally conserved, and many kinases enhance their activity by autophosphorylating their activation loop in response to stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 describe well-established knowledge about protein kinase function and regulation. These are foundational concepts in the field supported by extensive prior literature and are presented as background information rather than novel findings.

results.result: The mechanism of activation loop autophosphorylation is controversial, though kinases are classically thought to perform this reaction in trans via transient dimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 accurately describe the state of the field and the classical model. This sets up the central question addressed by the review and is supported by the extensive discussion of conflicting evidence throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The kinase domain has a conserved bi-lobal structure with ATP binding in the cleft between N- and C-lobes, with the glycine-rich loop organizing the γ-phosphate and the αD helix and activation loop governing substrate recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 describe the fundamental structural features of kinase domains, supported by citation to Knighton et al., 1991 and Figure 1A. This is well-established structural knowledge.

results.result: The αG helix mediates diverse protein-protein interactions including kinase domain dimerization, trans-autoinhibition, trans-autophosphorylation, binding of regulatory subunits, substrate recognition, and recruitment of protein phosphatases.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C17 are well-supported by multiple citations for each function. The multifunctional role of the αG helix is established through extensive prior work cited in the manuscript.

results.result: The active kinase conformation is characterized by assembly of hydrophobic C-spine and R-spine, a conserved lysine-glutamate salt bridge, and the catalytic spine linking ATP binding to αC helix orientation and αD helix formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 describe well-established structural features of active kinases, supported by citations to Kornev et al., Huse and Kuriyan, and Endicott et al., along with Figure 1B-C. This is foundational structural knowledge.

results.result: Some kinases like Akt/PKB are regulated by disorder-to-order transition of the activation loop upon phosphorylation, with the phosphorylated loop stabilized by hydrogen bonds and mutations affecting this coordination implicated in disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are supported by citations to Huse and Kuriyan 2002, Yang et al. 2002b, and George et al. 2004, along with Figure 1D showing the structural features. This describes an established regulatory mechanism.

results.result: DMPKs exhibit the active conformation constitutively in the absence of phosphorylation, representing kinases not regulated by activation loop phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 is supported by multiple citations demonstrating this property of DMPKs. This provides an important counterexample to the general principle of activation loop phosphorylation-dependent regulation.

results.result: In AGC kinases, substrate recognition involves salt bridges between conserved glutamate/aspartate residues in the αD helix and catalytic loop with arginine residues at P-3 and P-5 positions in the substrate.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by citation to Yang et al. 2002a and Figure 1E showing the structural basis of substrate recognition. This describes an established mechanism for AGC kinase substrate specificity.

results.result: Recent systematic screening of substrate specificities for all human serine/threonine kinases provides a resource for kinase biologists, with additional substrate recognition elements particularly well characterized for MAPKs.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 are supported by citations to Johnson et al. 2023, Miller and Turk 2018, and Sheridan et al. 2008. These describe recent and established resources for understanding kinase substrate specificity.

results.result: Phosphoryl-transfer is a dissociative elimination-addition reaction with kinases achieving up to 3×10^5 fold rate enhancement, with crystallographic and neutron diffraction evidence for transition states and product release mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 describe the catalytic mechanism supported by citations to Endicott et al., Lassila et al., Madhusudan et al., and Gerlits et al. This is well-established mechanistic knowledge about kinase catalysis.

results.result: Common methods to inactivate kinases include mutation of the β3 lysine or DFG aspartate (affecting ATP binding) or the catalytic aspartate to asparagine (the recommended approach), with each having potential unintended consequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 describe experimental approaches with their limitations, supported by citations to Eyers et al., Haydon et al., Iyer et al., and others. The recommendation for D→N mutation is based on structural reasoning (isosteric substitution) shown in Figure 1F.

results.result: Phosphomimetic substitutions have important limitations: aspartate/glutamate carry single negative charges versus two for phosphate, have different hydrogen bonding capacities, and differ in length from phosphoserine.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 describe chemical properties of amino acids and their limitations as phosphomimetics. This is established chemical knowledge presented as a cautionary note about experimental design.

results.result: The activation loop has the highest sequence divergence and greatest structural flexibility compared to the rest of the kinase domain fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by citations to Modi and Dunbrack 2019 and Nolen et al. 2004. This establishes the activation loop as a key regulatory element with high variability.

results.result: Multiple kinases employ activation loop-mediated autoinhibition: IRK adopts an ATP-incompatible conformation, Src family kinases sequester the autophosphorylation site with SH2/SH3 domain assistance and ADP stabilization, with individual members having additional regulatory mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C55 describe various autoinhibition mechanisms supported by multiple citations and Figure 2A-B. The diversity of mechanisms within related kinase families is well-documented in the cited literature.

results.result: CAMKs and related kinases are autoinhibited by C-terminal helices occupying the catalytic cleft, while PKA is inhibited in trans by its regulatory subunit presenting a pseudosubstrate, with Ca2+/CaM or cAMP binding relieving inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C61 describe steric occlusion mechanisms supported by multiple citations and Figure 2C-D. The relief of inhibition by second messengers is well-established.

results.result: DAPKs form face-to-face dimers that occlude catalytic clefts requiring Ca2+/CaM for activation, with an analogous trans-autoinhibited dimer reported for PKD.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by citations to Patel et al., Simon et al., and Reinhardt et al. 2023, along with Figure 2E. The PKD mechanism is from recent work by the authors.

results.result: B-Raf is maintained in an autoinhibited conformation by 14-3-3 proteins that create a cradle burying the CRD and preventing back-to-back dimerization required for MEK phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by citations to Park et al. 2019, Rajakulendran et al., and Wan et al., along with Figure 2F. This describes an allosteric autoinhibition mechanism.

results.result: AGC kinases have a ~50 amino acid C-terminal extension containing cis-regulatory elements including a hydrophobic motif that stabilizes the active conformation, with regulation by phosphorylation, phosphomimetics, regulatory domains, or protein co-factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 describe AGC kinase regulation supported by multiple citations and Figure 3A. This is a well-characterized activation mechanism with diverse regulatory inputs.

results.result: A hydrophobic motif was recently identified in PDK1, previously thought to lack this element, with the tail implicated in allosteric trans-autoactivation in PIP3-bound dimers.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by citation to Levina et al. 2022. This represents a recent discovery extending the AGC kinase regulatory paradigm to PDK1.

results.result: Aurora kinases are activated in trans by TPX2 (AurA) or INCENP (AurB) inserting hydrophobic motifs into the kinase domain, conceptually similar to cyclin-dependent kinase activation by cyclins.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 are supported by citations to Bayliss et al., Eyers et al., Sessa et al., and Wood and Endicott, along with Figure 3B. This describes trans-activation by accessory proteins.

results.result: PDK1 forms a transient face-to-face dimer upon binding to PIP3-containing membranes, illustrating trans-autophosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by citation to Levina et al. 2022 and Figure 3C. This provides an example of membrane-mediated dimerization facilitating trans-autophosphorylation.

results.result: Contradicting evidence for both cis and trans-phosphorylation mechanisms has been reported for multiple kinases including AurA, Chk2, IRAK4, IR kinase, and PKR.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 document the controversy in the field through multiple citations. This establishes the central problem addressed by the review: conflicting evidence about autophosphorylation mechanisms.

results.result: Models of cis-autophosphorylation have been proposed for GSK3β, DYRKs, and PKD, with PKD shown to be autoinhibited in trans and activated by cis-autophosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C90 are supported by citations including recent work by the authors (Reinhardt et al. 2023) and Figure 3D. The PKD mechanism represents a novel finding combining trans-autoinhibition with cis-autophosphorylation.

results.result: PKD, a non-HRD kinase with an HCD motif, is activated by phosphorylation with a different arginine replacing the canonical HRD arginine, and mass spectrometry demonstrates autophosphorylation occurs exclusively in cis.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 are supported by citations to Johnson et al., Nolen et al., and Reinhardt et al. 2023. The mass spectrometry evidence for exclusive cis-autophosphorylation is a key finding challenging the classical trans model.

results.result: PKR, IRE1, PERK, and NEK7 require back-to-back dimerization for activation by autophosphorylation, though whether this occurs in cis or requires higher-order oligomerization remains debated.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 are supported by multiple citations. This highlights another area of ongoing controversy about the relationship between dimerization and autophosphorylation mechanism.

results.result: B-Raf activation depends on back-to-back dimerization critical for MEK phosphorylation, with MEK forming a heterodimer with B-Raf homologous to PDK1 homodimers, and mutagenesis of the αG helix interface impairing both PDK1 and MEK activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 are supported by citations to Park et al., Rajakulendran et al., Wan et al., Levina et al., and Haling et al., along with Figures 3E-F. The mutagenesis data provides functional validation of the dimerization interfaces.

results.result: IKK family kinases (IKKε and TBK1) form constitutive back-to-back dimers via helical stalk and ubiquitin-like domains, with activation loop autophosphorylation proposed to occur via higher-order oligomerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by citations to Larabi et al., Tu et al., Xu et al., Zhang et al., and Zhao et al. This describes another example of back-to-back dimerization with uncertain autophosphorylation mechanism.

results.result: Intact mass spectrometry is precise to <1 Da up to 100-200 kDa and is an essential quality control step, with native MS capable of capturing ligand-bound species, protein-lipid interactions, and protein complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 describe mass spectrometry capabilities supported by multiple citations. This establishes the technical foundation for the authors' recommended experimental approaches.

results.result: Phosphorylation detection methods have important limitations: phosphorylation can hinder proteolytic cleavage in MS2, phospho-antibodies may recognize specific subpopulations, Western blotting is semi-quantitative at best, and many antibodies lack specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C112 describe technical limitations supported by citations to Waldron et al. and multiple papers on the antibody reproducibility crisis. This provides critical evaluation of common experimental approaches.

results.result: FGFR1 autophosphorylation of five sites was characterized by combining radionucleotide assays with time-resolved intact mass spectrometry to discriminate phosphorylation state dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by citation to Lew et al. 2009. This provides an example of successful integration of complementary techniques for studying autophosphorylation.

results.result: Concentration-dependent kinase activity is usually interpreted as trans but cannot distinguish between face-to-face trans, back-to-back cis, or higher-order mechanisms; decreased activity indicates trans-autoinhibition; concentration-independent reactions likely proceed in cis.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C117 provide logical analysis of concentration-dependence experiments supported by citations and Figure 4C. This critical evaluation highlights limitations of common interpretations.

results.result: The gold standard to discriminate cis from trans-autophosphorylation is testing whether active kinase can phosphorylate inactive kinase, though autophosphorylation motifs similar to substrate recognition motifs may be prone to trans-phosphorylation at high concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 describe the standard experimental approach with important caveats, shown in Figure 4D. This provides practical guidance while acknowledging potential artifacts.

results.result: Unimolecular cis-autophosphorylation is independent of concentration, diffusion, or substrate depletion, proceeding with constant catalytic rate until completion, resulting in linear kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 provide kinetic analysis of cis-autophosphorylation shown in Figure 5A. This is logical inference from first principles about unimolecular reactions.

results.result: Trans-autophosphorylation is a bimolecular reaction dependent on enzyme-substrate association, intrinsic catalytic rate, and product dissociation.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 provide kinetic analysis of trans-autophosphorylation. This is logical inference from first principles about bimolecular reactions.

results.result: Symmetric cis-autophosphorylation dependent on back-to-back dimerization is bimolecular and concentration-dependent, with collision of two unphosphorylated molecules resulting in phosphorylation of both.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 defines a specific reaction mechanism and its kinetic properties. This is logical inference about a dimerization-dependent cis mechanism shown in Figure 5B.

results.result: In symmetric trans-autophosphorylation, only homo-dimeric collisions are productive and the reaction rate decays with substrate depletion over time.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 provides kinetic analysis of symmetric trans-autophosphorylation shown in Figure 5C. This is logical inference about the consequences of activation loop stabilization upon phosphorylation.

results.result: Asymmetric trans-autophosphorylation involves one kinase as enzyme and one as substrate, limited by stochastic conformational sampling, with phosphorylation increasing catalytic efficiency, resulting in sigmoidal kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C127 provide kinetic analysis of asymmetric trans-autophosphorylation shown in Figure 5D. This is logical inference about a two-step mechanism with autocatalytic properties.

results.result: Transient kinase domain dimerization must be associated with local concentration mechanisms to overcome diffusion dependence for rapid signal transduction.
results.evaluation: Claim C128 is a logical inference about physiological requirements for trans-autophosphorylation. This connects in vitro observations to cellular context.

results.result: In constitutively dimeric kinases, bimolecular cis- and trans-autophosphorylation are reduced to unimolecular reactions with linear kinetics limited only by intrinsic catalytic rate.
results.evaluation: Claim C129 provides kinetic analysis shown in Figures 5E-F. This is logical inference about the consequences of constitutive dimerization eliminating concentration and diffusion dependence.

results.result: Kinetic data alone cannot necessarily discriminate between cis- and trans-autophosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 is a key conclusion from the kinetic analysis in the preceding claims. This highlights a major limitation of kinetic approaches for mechanistic discrimination.

results.result: Kinase dimerization must be transient with low binding free energy; if too strong, kinases become constitutively trapped in inhibited or active states.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 provide thermodynamic reasoning about regulatory requirements. This is logical inference about the constraints on dimerization for reversible regulation.

results.result: Individual kinase domains are still at the limits of current cryo-electron microscopy technology.
results.evaluation: Claim C133 is supported by citation to Herzik et al. 2019. This establishes why crystallography remains the primary structural method despite its limitations.

results.result: Crystal lattice formation requires specific contacts between molecules, driven by enthalpic gain and desolvation entropy, representing energetically favorable states that may misrepresent protein-protein contacts and require biochemical validation.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C138 describe crystallography principles supported by citations to Rupp 2009 and Krissinel 2010. This provides critical context for evaluating crystallographic evidence of dimerization.

results.result: Trans-autophosphorylation requires activation loop exchange between protomers, with the requirement for phosphorylation dictating that loops are flexible in the unphosphorylated state.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C140 provide logical inference about structural requirements for trans-autophosphorylation. This establishes why activation loops are prone to forming crystal contacts.

results.result: Chk2 crystals contain activation loop exchanges generating equivalent trans interactions as normally found in cis, with nitrate ions and non-physiological magnesium positions in the structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C143 describe the Chk2 crystal structure from Oliver et al. 2006 shown in Figure 6A-B. The presence of crystallization artifacts (nitrate, misplaced Mg2+) raises questions about physiological relevance.

results.result: Activation loop exchanges have been observed in many kinase crystal structures with highly variable protomer orientations likely reflecting lattice formation, including in kinases like DAPK3 that don't undergo autophosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C146 are supported by multiple citations. The observation of similar exchanges in non-autophosphorylating kinases strongly suggests these are crystallization artifacts rather than functional intermediates.

results.result: A longer Chk2 construct shows FHA domain-swapped dimers with face-to-face kinase domains, but confirmation as the trans-autophosphorylation intermediate was precluded by disordered activation loops and an ATP-binding mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C148 describe the Cai et al. 2009 structure shown in Figure 6C. The absence of activation loop density and use of an inactivating mutation prevent definitive conclusions about the autophosphorylation mechanism.

results.result: The Rad53 structure also used a kinase-inactivating mutation, and while one protomer superposes well with Chk2 (0.90 Å r.m.s.d.), the second chain differs dramatically (11.50 Å r.m.s.d.).
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C150 are supported by citation to Wybenga-Groot et al. 2014 with quantitative structural comparison. The large r.m.s.d. for the second chain undermines claims of structural similarity between Chk2 and Rad53 dimers.

results.result: Recent in silico modeling and biochemistry on PKD revealed a face-to-face trans-inhibited dimer.
results.evaluation: Claim C151 is supported by citation to Reinhardt et al. 2023 (authors' own work). This provides an alternative to the Chk2/Rad53 structures but lacks experimental structural validation.

results.result: For AurA, kinetic data points to cis-autophosphorylation, but crystal structures suggest trans; however, the Zorba et al. structure lacks catalytic site magnesium ions, has the catalytic aspartate out of position, and likely represents a crystallization artifact.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C155 provide critical analysis of conflicting AurA data, with detailed structural examination shown in Figure 6D. The identification of the structure as incompatible with phosphoryl transfer is a key insight.

results.result: AurA has been proposed as a redox-sensitive switch inhibited by CoA or activated by ROS, but biochemical studies show oxidation inactivates AurA irrespective of activation loop phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C158 are supported by citations to Tsuchiya et al., Lim et al., and Byrne et al. This highlights additional complexity and conflicting interpretations in the AurA literature.

results.result: A kinase requiring activation loop phosphorylation for catalytic competence must somehow perform this reaction without being phosphorylated, implying the autophosphorylation reaction is mechanistically distinct from substrate phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C160 articulate the central paradox of activation loop autophosphorylation shown in Figure 8A. This is a logical inference that frames the fundamental problem.

results.result: Consensus autophosphorylation motifs often don't resemble substrate recognition motifs, and a PKD separation-of-function mutant disrupting substrate recognition had no effect on cis-autophosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C161 and C163 are supported by citations to Beenstock et al. and Reinhardt et al. 2023, with data shown in Figure 8B. The PKD mutant provides experimental evidence that autophosphorylation is mechanistically distinct.

results.result: Kinases have low nanomolar abundance in cells with high protein concentrations (200-300 mg/ml), and by diffusion alone proteins undergo <0.1 interactions with another copy in their lifetime, requiring coordinated assembly for bimolecular reactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C167 are supported by citations to Hein et al. and Batada et al., with data shown in Figure 8C. This establishes the cellular context constraining trans-autophosphorylation mechanisms.

results.result: Many receptor tyrosine kinases exist as pre-formed inactive dimers activated by ligand-induced conformational changes, while other kinases are locally concentrated on membranes by lipid second messenger binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C170 are supported by multiple citations. This describes cellular mechanisms that overcome diffusion limitations for trans-autophosphorylation.

results.result: Early kinetic data indicated IRK autophosphorylation could occur in both cis and trans, but structural and biochemical studies of IGFR1 and FGFR3 concluded the reaction occurs in trans.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C172 are supported by multiple citations documenting the evolution of understanding about insulin receptor family autophosphorylation. This sets up the detailed structural analysis that follows.

results.result: Crystal structures show IGFR1 in a symmetric trans dimer with both activation loops in opposing active sites, FGFR3 in an asymmetric trans dimer with one activation loop in the opposing active site, and IGFR1 in a different asymmetric dimer.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C175 are supported by citations to Wu et al., Chen et al., Nemecek et al., and Xu et al., with structures shown in Figures 8D-E. The structural diversity raises questions about which, if any, represents the physiological mechanism.

results.result: Two-step trans-autophosphorylation mechanisms have been proposed for PAK and IRAK4 based on crystal structures, and IRAK1 has been proposed to form heterodimers with phosphorylated IRAK4.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C177 are supported by citations to Ferrao et al., Wang et al. 2011, and Wang et al. 2017. This extends the diversity of proposed trans mechanisms.

results.result: The activation loop adopts the same conformation in cis, trans symmetric, trans asymmetric, and trans substrate structures with tyrosine poised for phosphoryl transfer, demonstrating all reactions are stereochemically possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C179 provide structural analysis shown in Figure 8H. This is a key insight that stereochemical compatibility doesn't prove physiological relevance.

results.result: What we observe in crystal lattices and in vitro does not necessarily reflect reality in the cell, depending on factors like local concentration and conformational sampling.
results.evaluation: Claim C180 is the central cautionary message of the review. This is a logical conclusion from the extensive analysis of conflicting structural and biochemical evidence.
